dd7c6fd7bb.why: 'A part of a living thing' is gone, so 'A habitat' is live again ('where it lives' even lures toward it). 'A learned skill' is a real 5th-grade confusion. Beak, shell and spines are inherited body features; an instinct and a learned skill are behaviours, and a habitat is a place.

7bdcbe11d7.why: 'Many other water birds' fixes the precision note: grebes and coots have lobed toes. Webbing is inherited and forms in the embryo before hatching. The three lures are the use, wanting and environment misconceptions, all wrong.

a0fd1358f8.why: Flagged risk checked. Mountain goats have 'subcutaneous fat reserves' (Grokipedia) and yaks lay down fat under the skin before winter (FAO), but neither is blubber. Blubber is the marine mammals' insulating layer against cold water, thickest in polar species, and the pairing of blubber and dense fur is the polar bear's, an animal of the sea ice. So 'Snowy mountain peaks' is a fair lure, not a second answer, and the context's 'mainly with thick, woolly coats' stays true. The old tell (the only cold place) is fixed.

cf53b403b1.why: Hibernation and migration, which the stem ruled out, are replaced with mimicry and moulting, which it cannot rule out. Background matching is crypsis (camouflage), while mimicry needs misidentification as a specific thing (Grokipedia), so there is one answer. Hoverflies are Batesian wasp mimics, and moulting is the shedding of skin, feathers or fur. Only 'Warning colours' is still weakened by 'never spots it', which is acceptable.

e7b03bbb46.why: The context no longer states the false all-animal-eaters rule, and the ants choice is gone. Shrews have sharp spike-like teeth and eat beetles and earthworms; foxes hunt rabbits and mice; bears pair broad flat molars with prominent hooked canines and eat berries and fish. 'Berries and fish' now makes the missing long front teeth decide, so the plants-or-animals odd-one-out is fixed. Horses have flat, ridged molars.

020c21c540.why: 'In its leaves' is the real confusion (fleshy pads taken for leaves) and is truly wrong. Stems are the cactus's water reservoirs and its ribs let it swell; spines are modified leaves; leaves are absent or reduced in most cacti (Pereskia aside), so 'Most cacti' is right; roots are shallow and spreading.

a92137039d.why: Stem tell, and the overlap is not cleared. The stem puts the shallow roots 'just under the ground' and asks what the deep root reaches 'that the shallow ones cannot'. That rules out both surface choices (rain soon after it falls, dew on the sand) by the stem's own logic. The one remaining lure, 'Food stored deep in the soil', falls to roots-stems-leaves-and-flowers' keyed fact (roots take in water, not food, with the same 'food from the soil' lure). So the old fact plus 'deep' still decides it, as the judge warned. The facts themselves are true.

749ce02e50.why: All three lures now sound like real winter reasons, and each is wrong. Next year's buds form at the end of summer, so the old leaves need not make room. Frost cracks appear in winter on deciduous trees with thin bark, bare or not. A leafless tree pulls up less water, not more. The key is true: shedding cuts transpiration while the ground's liquid water is scarce.
